newsitem.title: USA: Calif. electricity plan seen boosting utility stocks.
newsitem.headline: Calif. electricity plan seen boosting utility stocks.

text.p: Legislation to open California's electricity market to competition passed this weekend, removing some uncertainty regarding California utilities' most costly investments.
The new law is expected to boost stocks of California utility companies.

"Stock prices started to recover once we learned that the plan included a special class of bonds that would finance and buy out stranded costs," said Barry Abramson at Prudential Securities. "That reduces a lot of the financial risk."
But he and other experts question whether the California utilities will be able to keep significant market share under competition.
These utilities include Edison International's Southern California Edison, Pacific Gas and Electric and Enova Corp.'s San Diego Gas and Electric.

The legislation ends the system under which customers had to obtain service through a designated utility, guaranteeing that utility a regulated profit. The new law replaces this system by allowing customers to choose their electricity supplier no later than Jan. 1 1998.
But it also requires power consumers to pay through 2001 a charge that will be used to fund the utilities' stranded investments, such as high-cost nuclear power plants.
This requirement would remove a lot of utility investor concerns.

"This removes a lot of the uncertainty ... risk is shared between ratepayers and shareholders," said Doug Christopher, an analyst at Crowell Weedon. "The regulatory, political environment is not as extreme as we once thought."

Wall Street reacted badly to the initial April 1994 proposal by the California Public Utilities Commission to deregulate the state's electricity industry, sending utility stock and bond prices sharply lower. But most of these stocks have moved higher in the last two weeks in anticipation of the law, which would remove uncertainty about these costs.
Edison's stock ended at $17.375 Friday, up from the low teens in April 1994, while PG&E was at $22.625, up from 20 last week. Enova closed Friday at $22.875, compared with $20.875 earlier in August.

"Having legislative endorsement for the recovery of stranded assets is positive," said Sam Brothwell, a debt analyst at Moody's Investors Service. "But the legislation does not define the dollar amount of the past investments."
Under the plan, the transition charge will be levied on all consumers, but smaller users are protected from bearing a non-proportional share of the costs.
"The principal risk is the folks on the other side of the table," noted Brothwell. "The CTC (competitive transition charge) stands between them and cheaper electricity."
Electricity customers obviously want the CTC as low as possible, while the utilities want it as high as possible.

Abrahamson noted uncertainties also remain about how an open market will function and whether the transition period set by the state will hold. "If the market realities come down faster, it is unclear if this plan can work under a multi-year period," he said.
